extracted.intended_audience: immigration attorneys, petitioners/applicants for E (treaty trader/investor) and F (student) nonimmigrant classifications, and USCIS adjudicators
extracted.subtask_short: E and F nonimmigrant eligibility rules
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory standards and documentary/evidentiary criteria governing eligibility, maintenance, change, and admission procedures for E (treaty trader/investor, including CNMI special rules) and F-1 student nonimmigrant classifications under USCIS regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on employment for E treaty status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Service determines the terms and conditions of E treaty status at the time of admission or approval of a request to change nonimmigrant status to E classification. A treaty trader, treaty investor, or treaty employee may engage only in employment which is consistent with the terms and conditions of his or her status and the activity forming the basis for the E treaty status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employment must be consistent with the terms/activities forming the basis for the E classification as determined at admission or status-approval; deviations can implicate substantive change rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subsidiary employment — evidentiary requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Treaty employees may perform work for the parent treaty organization or enterprise, or any subsidiary of the parent organization or enterprise. Performing work for subsidiaries of a common parent enterprise or organization will not be deemed to constitute a substantive change if, at the time E status was determined, the applicant presented evidence establishing the enterprise/subsidiaries, parent-subsidiary relationship, and that the subsidiary independently qualifies as a treaty organization or enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Required evidence includes identification of enterprise and subsidiaries, proof of parent-subsidiary relationship, and demonstration that the subsidiary qualifies independently; for employees of traders/investors the work must require executive, supervisory, or essential skills; work must be consistent with the original terms/conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive change requiring new approval
rubrics_metrics.description: Approval of USCIS must be obtained when there will be a substantive change in the terms or conditions of E status. The treaty alien must file a new application requesting extension of stay and evidence of continued eligibility, or obtain a visa reflecting new terms and seek admission accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: USCIS will deem changes such as a fundamental change in the employing entity's basic characteristics (e.g., merger, acquisition, or sale of the division where the alien is employed) to be substantive and necessitating a new application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-substantive changes — no prior approval required
rubrics_metrics.description: Neither prior approval nor a new application is required if there is no substantive, or fundamental, change in the terms or conditions of the alien's employment that would affect eligibility for E classification. Corporate changes that do not affect the previously approved employment relationship or are otherwise non-substantive do not require prior approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To facilitate admission an alien may (A) present a letter from the treaty-qualifying company explaining the change; (B) request a new approval notice by filing an application describing the change; or (C) apply to Department of State for a new E visa. If none of these are elected, the alien may otherwise demonstrate admissibility to the inspecting immigration officer at port-of-entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting USCIS advice on whether change is substantive
rubrics_metrics.description: To request advice from USCIS as to whether a change is substantive, an alien may file an application with a complete description of the change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases involving multiple employees, file a single application attaching a list of related receipt numbers and an explanation of the change(s) to request a determination on whether separate applications are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approval notice and employment authorization upon change approval
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application to change the terms and conditions of E status or employment is approved, USCIS will notify the applicant on Form I-797. An extension of stay may be granted for the validity of the approved application. The alien is not authorized to begin the new employment until the application is approved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employment authorization exists only for the period the alien remains in the United States; readmission in E classification after departure may require presentation of unexpired E visa and Form I-797 or compliance with 22 CFR 41.112(d) for short contiguous-territory absences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unauthorized change of employment — failure to maintain status
rubrics_metrics.description: An unauthorized change of employment to a new employer will constitute a failure to maintain status within the meaning of section 237(a)(1)(C)(i) of the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In all cases where a treaty employee will be providing services to a subsidiary, the subsidiary must comply with the terms of 8 CFR part 274a (employment authorization/payroll rules).

rubrics_metrics.name: Items of trade — definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Items of trade include but are not limited to goods, services, international banking, insurance, monies, transportation, communications, data processing, advertising, accounting, design and engineering, management consulting, tourism, technology and its transfer, and some news-gathering activities. Goods are tangible commodities or merchandise having extrinsic value. Services are legitimate economic activities which provide other than tangible goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples provided are illustrative, not exhaustive; services must be legitimate economic activities rather than mere domestic activities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade — definition and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Trade is the existing international exchange of items of trade for consideration between the United States and the treaty country. Existing trade includes successfully negotiated contracts binding upon the parties which call for the immediate exchange of items of trade. Domestic trade or the development of domestic markets without international exchange does not constitute trade for purposes of E classification. The exchange must be traceable and identifiable and title to the trade item must pass from one treaty party to the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must show international exchange for consideration with traceable transactions and passing of title; planned or speculative domestic activity without international exchange is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial trade — continuity and transaction volume
rubrics_metrics.description: Substantial trade is an amount of trade sufficient to ensure a continuous flow of international trade items between the United States and the treaty country. This continuous flow contemplates numerous transactions over time; treaty trader status may not be established or maintained on the basis of a single transaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While monetary value is relevant, greater weight is given to numerous exchanges of larger value. There is no per-transaction monetary minimum. For smaller businesses, cumulative income from numerous transactions sufficient to support the trader and family is a favorable factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal trade — >50% volume test
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal trade between the United States and the treaty country exists when over 50 percent of the volume of international trade of the treaty trader is conducted between the United States and the treaty country of the trader's nationality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Volume is measured as the trader's international trade volume; principal trade requires a majority share (>50%) with the treaty country.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investment — definition and elements
rubrics_metrics.description: An investment is the treaty investor's placing of capital, including funds and other assets, at risk in the commercial sense with the objective of generating a profit. The treaty investor must be in possession of and have control over the capital invested or being invested. The capital must be subject to partial or total loss if investment fortunes reverse and must be irrevocably committed to the enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alien bears burden of establishing irrevocable commitment; legal mechanisms (e.g., escrow) that irrevocably commit funds and may extend personal liability protection are permissible. Capital must not be derived from criminal activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bona fide enterprise
rubrics_metrics.description: The enterprise must be a real, active, and operating commercial or entrepreneurial undertaking which produces services or goods for profit and must meet applicable legal requirements for doing business in the particular jurisdiction in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial or non-operational entities that do not produce goods/services for profit will not qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial amount of capital — three-pronged test
rubrics_metrics.description: A substantial amount of capital constitutes an amount which is: (i) substantial in relationship to the total cost of either purchasing an established enterprise or creating the type of enterprise under consideration; (ii) sufficient to ensure the treaty investor's financial commitment to the successful operation of the enterprise; and (iii) of a magnitude to support the likelihood that the treaty investor will successfully develop and direct the enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally, the lower the total cost of the enterprise, the higher, proportionately, the investment must be. No absolute dollar threshold is stated here; analysis is relative to enterprise cost and needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Marginal enterprise — prohibition and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: An enterprise may not be marginal. A marginal enterprise is one that does not have the present or future capacity to generate more than enough income to provide a minimal living for the treaty investor and family. An enterprise that lacks capacity to generate such income but has present or future capacity to make a significant economic contribution is not marginal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Projected future income-generating capacity should generally be realizable within 5 years of commencement of normal business activity. Evidence of significant economic contribution may rebut marginal classification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solely to develop and direct — control requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien seeking classification as a treaty investor (or owner of the treaty enterprise) must demonstrate that he or she does or will develop and direct the investment enterprise, and must establish control either by ownership of at least 50 percent, by possessing operational control through a managerial position or other corporate device, or by other means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate majority ownership or operational managerial control; corporate documents, titles, and duties should show control.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive and supervisory character — primary duties
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant's position must be principally and primarily executive or supervisory in nature. Executive duties provide ultimate control and responsibility for the enterprise's overall operation or a major component thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators consider: (i) authority to determine policy/direction; (ii) supervisory responsibility for a significant proportion of operations (not limited to direct supervision of low-level employees); and (iii) possession of executive/supervisory skills and experience, salary and title commensurate with such duties, recognition as a position of authority, responsibility for discretionary decisions, policy-setting, direction and management of business operations, and supervision of professional personnel. Routine staff work must be incidental only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special qualifications — essential skills test
rubrics_metrics.description: Special qualifications are skills/aptitudes that an employee in a lesser capacity brings to a position or role that are essential to the successful or efficient operation of the treaty enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjudicators evaluate: (i) degree of proven expertise, uniqueness of skill relative to others, length of experience/training, period required to perform duties effectively, relation of skill to enterprise processes, and salary such qualifications command (language/culture knowledge alone insufficient); and (ii) whether such skills are readily available in the United States. Consider time-limited essentiality (e.g., start-up training) and request evidence of period skills will be needed where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Period of admission for treaty trader/investor
rubrics_metrics.description: A treaty trader or treaty investor may be admitted for an initial period of not more than 2 years. Spouse and minor children are admitted for the period during which the principal is in valid treaty trader or investor status. An alien shall not be admitted in E classification for a period extending more than 6 months beyond the expiration date of the alien's passport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Initial admission limited to up to 2 years; passport validity can constrain admission length.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extensions of stay for E classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for extensions of stay may be granted in increments of not more than 2 years. A treaty trader or investor in valid E status may apply for extension by filing the prescribed form with required documents per §214.1 and form instructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility for extension requires proof that the alien: (A) has at all times maintained the terms and conditions of E classification; (B) was physically present in the United States at the time of filing; and (C) has not abandoned the extension request. Employees with special qualifications responsible for start-up operations are presumed able to complete objectives within 2 years and absent special circumstances will not be eligible for extension. There is no specified number of extensions subject to paragraph limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change of nonimmigrant status to E
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien in another valid nonimmigrant status may apply for change of status to E classification by filing the prescribed form with required accompanying documents establishing eligibility, in accordance with 8 CFR part 248.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spouse/minor children file concurrent applications for derivative treaty classification; such derivative applications are approved only if principal is granted and maintains treaty status, and are approved for the period of admission authorized for the principal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denial of E status to Canadians/Mexicans in certain labor disputes
rubrics_metrics.description: A citizen of Canada or Mexico may be denied E treaty trader or investor status if: (A) the Secretary of Labor certifies or informs USCIS that a strike or other labor dispute involving a work stoppage of workers in the alien's occupational classification is in progress at the place of intended employment; and (B) temporary entry of that alien may adversely affect settlement of the dispute or employment of persons involved in the dispute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an alien has commenced employment and is participating in a strike, such participation alone will not constitute failure to maintain status solely on account of strike participation, but the alien remains subject to all INA provisions. If the strike is not certified and USCIS not informed, the Commissioner shall not deny entry to an applicant for E status on that basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: E-2 CNMI Investor — eligibility criteria (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: During the specified period an alien may be classified as a CNMI-only E-2 nonimmigrant treaty investor if the alien: (A) was lawfully admitted to CNMI in long-term investor status under CNMI immigration laws before the transition program effective date and had that status on the transition date; (B) has continuously maintained residence in CNMI; (C) is otherwise admissible to the United States; and (D) maintains the investment(s) that formed the basis for long-term investment status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligibility is tied to prior CNMI long-term investor classifications and continued maintenance of investments and residency per CNMI law; deadlines and transition period restrictions apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNMI-specific definitions (approved investment/letter/certificate/continuous residence/transition period)
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions applicable to CNMI E-2 provisions: 'Approved investment or residence' means approved by CNMI government; 'Approval letter' certifies acceptance subject to CNMI minimum investment criteria; 'Certificate' means CNMI government-issued approval certificate; 'Continuously maintained residence' requires residence since lawful admission and physical presence totaling at least half the time with absence rules (breaks continuity if >6 months but <1 year unless proven not abandoned; break if >=1 year); 'Transition period' defined as beginning on transition program effective date and ending on December 31, 2029.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuity-of-residence rules include specific absence thresholds; applicants must supply evidence to overcome presumptive breaks in continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNMI long-term investor status categories and monetary thresholds
rubrics_metrics.description: Long-term investor status under CNMI law includes: (A) Long-term business investor — approved investment of at least $50,000; (B) Foreign investor — invested either a minimum of $100,000 in aggregate approved investment in excess of $2,000,000, or $250,000 in a single approved investment; (C) Retiree investor — age over 55 and specific investment minimums depending on island ($100,000 Saipan or $75,000 Tinian/Rota) or $150,000 in approved residence to live in CNMI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These thresholds are CNMI-specific statutory standards used to determine prior long-term investor status eligibility under CNMI law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining CNMI investments — compliance requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien in long-term investor status under CNMI immigration laws is maintaining investments if that alien is in compliance with the terms upon which the investor certificate was issued.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compliance means adhering to conditions of the CNMI-issued certificate; failure to do so may negate eligibility for E-2 CNMI status.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNMI filing procedures and deadline
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien seeking E-2 CNMI classification must file an application and accompanying evidence with USCIS in accordance with form instructions before January 18, 2013. Applications filed after the filing date deadline will be rejected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict filing deadline — late filings are rejected; follow form instructions carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentary evidence required for E-2 CNMI eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Documentary evidence required includes: valid passport and properly endorsed CNMI admission document; unexpired CNMI investor certificates (Long-Term Business Certificate, Foreign Investment Certificate, or Foreign Retiree Investment Certificate) as applicable; evidence that long-term investor is maintaining investment (approval letter, bank statements, invoices, receipts, contracts for assets, stock purchase records, loan agreements, leases, financial statements, tax receipts, other agreements, evidence of minimum investment amounts, comprehensive business plan for new enterprises, articles of incorporation/by-laws, partnership agreements, corporate minutes, business licenses, foreign business registration records, recent tax returns, listing of employees, listing of holders of business certificates, listing of all corporations in which applicant has controlling interest, annual reports and independent CPA audit reports for certificate holders, and retiree-specific property evidence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive documentary package expected; list is detailed and specific to establishment, proof of capital, corporate structure, and ongoing compliance and may include audits for certificate holders.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNMI physical presence rule at filing and readmission constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical presence in CNMI at the time of filing or during pendency is not required, but an application may not be filed by, or E-2 CNMI status granted to, any alien present in U.S. territory other than in CNMI. If an alien with CNMI long-term investor status departs CNMI on or after the transition date but before being granted E-2 CNMI status, he or she may not be re-admitted to CNMI without a visa or appropriate inadmissibility waiver. If USCIS grants status to an alien not physically present in CNMI at time of grant, the alien must obtain an E-2 CNMI Investor visa at a consular office abroad to seek admission to CNMI in E-2 CNMI status.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Careful attention to where applicant is physically located at filing and at grant; readmission and visa requirements differ from general E-2 rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNMI background checks and biometrics
rubrics_metrics.description: USCIS may require an applicant for E-2 CNMI Investor status (including derivative spouse/child applicants) to submit biometrics as required under 8 CFR 103.16.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to provide biometrics as part of adjudication process.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNMI discretionary denial and right of appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: A grant of E-2 CNMI Investor status is discretionary, and the application may be denied for failure to demonstrate eligibility or for other good cause. Denial may be appealed to the USCIS Administrative Appeals Office or any successor body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discretionary nature means meeting eligibility does not guarantee approval; appeals available per USCIS procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spouse and children of E-2 CNMI Investor — classification and employment authorization
rubrics_metrics.description: The spouse and children of an E-2 CNMI Investor accompanying or following-to-join the principal, if otherwise admissible, may receive the same classification as the principal. The nationality of a spouse or child is not material. The spouse (other than spouse of investor who obtained status based on a Foreign Retiree Investment Certificate) is eligible to apply for employment authorization while in E-2 CNMI status; such authorization is limited to employment in the CNMI only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employment authorization for spouses is CNMI-limited and may be restricted where principal's status derived from retiree investment certificate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms and conditions of E-2 CNMI nonimmigrant status
rubrics_metrics.description: E-2 CNMI Investor nonimmigrant status and derivative status are only applicable in the CNMI. Entry, employment, and residence in the rest of the United States (including Guam) require the appropriate visa or visa waiver eligibility. Employment authorization is limited to the enterprise that is the basis for the CNMI certificate to the extent the certificate authorized such activity. Changes in substantive compliance require filing a new application; unauthorized change of employment constitutes failure to maintain status; periods of admission and extensions have CNMI-specific rules and constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CNMI E-2 status is territorially limited; travel or employment outside CNMI requires separate authorization. Substantive changes trigger new-application requirement similarly to general E rules. Extensions only up to transition period end; initial admissions up to two years.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNMI extensions of stay — eligibility criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for extensions of E-2 CNMI status may be granted in increments of not more than two years, until the end of the transition period. To qualify for an extension, each alien must demonstrate: (A) continuous maintenance of the terms and conditions of E-2 CNMI status; (B) physical presence in CNMI at the time of filing; and (C) that he or she did not leave during the pendency of the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical presence in CNMI at filing is required for CNMI extensions (unlike some general E rules). Extensions cannot be granted beyond transition period expiration.

rubrics_metrics.name: CNMI change of status procedures reference
rubrics_metrics.description: An alien lawfully admitted to the United States in another valid nonimmigrant status who is continuing to maintain that status may apply to change nonimmigrant status to E-2 CNMI Investor in accordance with paragraph (e)(21) of this section, if otherwise eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-reference to change-of-status procedures; eligibility includes prior CNMI long-term investor status when relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expiration of the transition period
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon expiration of the transition period, the E-2 CNMI Investor nonimmigrant status will automatically terminate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants/holders must track the transition period end date (December 31, 2029) and plan accordingly; cannot rely on CNMI E-2 status beyond that date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver of inadmissibility for CNMI applicants present in CNMI
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant for E-2 CNMI Investor status who is otherwise eligible and admissible and who has provided appropriate documents may be granted a waiver of inadmissibility under section 212(d)(3)(A)(ii) of the Act (including certain grounds tied solely to presence in CNMI on Nov 28, 2009) for the purpose of granting E-2 CNMI status. Such waiver may be granted without additional form or fee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appropriate supporting documents differ for spouse/child applicants present in CNMI (e.g., valid passport and evidence of lawful presence in CNMI under section 1806(e) of title 48). Waiver may be granted administratively without extra fee.

rubrics_metrics.name: F-1 student admission — eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonimmigrant student may be admitted in F-1 status if: (A) the student presents a Form I-20 or successor form issued in the student's name by a school certified by SEVP; (B) the student has documentary evidence of financial support in the amount indicated on the Form I-20; (C) for initial admission only, the student intends to attend the school specified in the visa or Form I-20; and (D) for public secondary school attendance, the student has reimbursed the local educational agency for the full unsubsidized per capita cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must have valid Form I-20 from SEVP-certified school and matching financial evidence; initial-admission intent to attend the listed school is required; public secondary school attendance has reimbursement rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form I-20 requirements at port-of-entry
rubrics_metrics.description: When an F-1 student applies for admission with a complete Form I-20 or successor form, the inspecting officer will transcribe the student's admission number from Form I-94 onto the Form I-20 (for initial admission only), endorse the Form I-20, and return it to the student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the Form I-20 for admission endorsements; officer will perform specified actions upon inspection at port-of-entry.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEVIS use and school obligations
rubrics_metrics.description: Schools must issue a Form I-20 or successor form in SEVIS to any current student requiring a reportable action (e.g., extension of stay, practical training, and requests for employment authorization), or to any alien who must obtain a new nonimmigrant student visa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designated School Officials must maintain SEVIS records and issue Forms I-20 in SEVIS for reportable events; timely updates are required for students' immigration status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student maintenance of Form I-20
rubrics_metrics.description: An F-1 student is expected to retain for safekeeping the initial Form I-20 bearing the admission number and any subsequent Form I-20 issued. If the student loses their current Form I-20, a replacement copy bearing the same information, including endorsements for employment/notational endorsements, should be issued by the DSO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should safeguard original I-20s; DSOs can issue replacement copies with identical information if loss occurs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admission of spouse and minor children of F-1 student
rubrics_metrics.description: The spouse and minor children accompanying an F-1 student are eligible for admission in F-2 status if the student is admitted in F-1 status. Spouse and children following-to-join are eligible for F-2 if they can demonstrate the F-1 student has been admitted and is, or will be within 30 days, enrolled in a full course of study or engaged in approved practical training following completion of studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derivative admission depends on principal's active enrollment or approved practical training and timeliness (within 30 days for following-to-join).
